OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Do all pairs of consecutive powerful numbers $n$ and $n+1$ come from solutions to Pell equations? In other words, must either $n$ or $n+1$ be a square?
Is the number of such $n\leq x$ bounded by $(\log x)^{O(1)}$?
#365: [Er76d,p.31][ErGr80,p.68]
number theory | 
powerful
Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=2^3y^2+1$. 
The list of $n$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful is A060355 in the OEIS.
The answer to the first question is no: Golomb [Go70] observed that both $12167=23^3$ and $12168=2^33^213^2$ are powerful. Walker [Wa76] proved that the equation\[7^3x^2=3^3y^2+1\]has infinitely many solutions, giving infinitely many counterexamples.
See also [364].
This is discussed in problem B16 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

In this 2017 paper of Aktas and Murty the upper bound of $O(x^{2/5})$ is obtained for the problem. As far as I can tell this is still the best known bound.

 In "Sentance, W. A. (1981). Occurrences of Consecutive Odd Powerful Numbers. The American Mathematical Monthly, 88(4), 272–274. https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.1981.11995246", the author has proved that "there exists an infinite number of pairs of consecutive odd powerful numbers, for eg: (25,27), each pair being associated with a certain Pell equation".
Also, in "https://www.fq.math.ca/Scanned/20-1/mcdaniel.pdf", W. L. McDaniel disproves a conjecture made by Golomb in [Go70] who conjectured that conjectured that "there are infinitely many integers that cannot be written as the difference of two powerful numbers.

 The Sentance paper proves that, every pair of powerful $n-1,n+1$ is associated with the solution of a Pell equation.
The latter is trivial:
$n$ has to be even and $n^2-1$ is powerful itself, so by definition of the form $my^2$ where $m \mid y.$
Nevertheless, the difference 2 result is not related to the difference 1 question.
